context.text: By the eighth century the holy icons filled Orthodox churches and homes. Emperor Leo III, a soldier from the eastern frontier, ruling an empire battered by Arab conquest, came to see their veneration as idolatry provoking God's wrath, and moved against them from 726, when the image of Christ over the palace's Chalke Gate was taken down.

narrative.text: Leo's edicts and his son Constantine V's zeal turned iconoclasm into imperial policy. A large but uncanonical synod at Hieria (754), no patriarch present, declared images of Christ impossible: to depict his humanity, it argued, either divides him or circumscribes his divinity. Icons were whitewashed and burned; the monks, iconodulia's fiercest defenders, bore the persecution, the monk Stephen the Younger, killed in 765, chief among its martyrs.

From Damascus, safely outside the emperor's reach under the caliphate, John of Damascus wrote the three Treatises on the Divine Images that armed the Church's answer: 'I do not venerate matter; I venerate the Creator of matter, who for my sake became matter.' The unseen God cannot be depicted, but the Word made flesh was seen, and what was seen may be shown. To refuse the icon is, at bottom, to doubt the Incarnation.

significance.text: Iconoclasm forced the Church to articulate why images belong to the Gospel itself: the icon is the confession of the Incarnation in line and color. The theology hammered out under this persecution stands behind every icon in every Orthodox church.
